Project 1 · Machine learning · Live online

Customer Churn Prediction API

"Which customers are about to leave — and can a model warn us in time?"

Live on Vercel

The problem

Telecom companies lose revenue when subscribers churn. Given a customer's usage and billing pattern, predict the probability they leave — early enough to act.

Approach

Cleaned and encoded the dataset, engineered features, and trained a scikit-learn pipeline — judged on ROC AUC and accuracy on held-out data, not training scores.

Implementation

The model was serialised and wrapped in a FastAPI service with /health and /predict endpoints, deployed to Vercel. Going live meant fixing a real bug: Vercel's rewrites replaced the request path, so no route matched — removing them let native routing serve the endpoints.

Result

A live, public ML API, verified end-to-end after deployment — health check green, model loaded, and a test prediction matching the local run.

Project 2 · Deep learning · Neural networks

Anomaly Detection Autoencoder

"Teach a neural network what normal looks like — then let it point at everything that isn't."

Work in progress

The idea

An autoencoder copies its input to its output through a narrow bottleneck, so it must learn the structure of normal data. Feed it something abnormal and the copy comes back wrong — that reconstruction error is the anomaly score.

Where it stands

Model and training code are built and public on GitHub. The hosted deployment failed before and is being reworked — it's in progress, not finished.

Why it matters

My bridge from classical ML into deep learning: same discipline, but the network learns the features itself instead of me engineering them by hand.

What it detects

Anything that doesn't fit normal: fraud-like transactions, faulty sensors, defective items — one technique, many domains.

HOW TO READ IT: the network compresses a signal down to a 2-node latent code, then rebuilds it. Normal data rebuilds cleanly. Anomalies don't — and the size of the error is the alarm.

STACK: PYTHON · NEURAL NETWORKS · ENCODER–DECODER ARCHITECTURE

Deep learning, in plain pictures

What I'm learning now, in two pictures — signals moving through a network, and a network learning what "normal" looks like.

Picture 1 · Inside a neural network

Signals, weights, decisions

Every line is a weight, every node a small calculation. Stack enough layers and the network discovers its own features instead of needing hand-made ones — that shift is what deep learning means.

Picture 2 · What the model sees vs. what it rebuilds

How the autoencoder "sees"

Original signalNetwork's reconstruction

Paired bars, one per measurement. Where the colours agree, the data is normal. Where they split, the error spikes — that's the anomaly alarm from Project 2.
